title: Animation Systems - Vertices, Cages, Rigs, Deformation, and Motion
abstract: A representation-first guide to vertex and cage animation, rigs and skinning, FK/IK and retargeting, skin and muscle deformation, hair simulation, facial controls, and runtime transformations.
image: /content/blog/Animation Systems - Vertices, Cages, Rigs, Deformation, and Motion/animation-systems.svg
imageAlt: One character mesh progresses from vertex samples and a control cage through a skeleton, muscles, hair strands, facial shapes, and a motion trajectory
lede: Animation systems differ mainly in what they control: final vertices, a surrounding cage, a joint hierarchy, physical tissue, strands, semantic facial shapes, or time-varying transforms. This guide preserves the supplied vocabulary—including the ambiguous term GX—adds the missing production concepts around it, and connects each group to foundational documentation, primary papers, equations, and current AI research without treating learned output as a substitute for runtime contracts.

sections.heading: Vertex-based animation: move the final samples
paragraphs: Vertex-based animation stores or computes the deformed position of each mesh vertex directly. It represents arbitrary motion—including cloth, fluid surfaces, destruction, and scanned performance—but depends on stable vertex identity when frames are interpolated or compressed.

Mesh caches keep explicit positions; morph targets store deltas from a base mesh; vertex animation textures move per-frame data into textures for GPU playback. All three trade rig editability for faithful reproduction of the sampled surface.

terms: Each weight w_k scales one per-vertex target delta.

sections.heading: Cage-based animation: deform through coordinates
paragraphs: A cage surrounds the detailed mesh with a small set of control vertices. Each embedded point is expressed as coordinates relative to the cage, so moving the coarse control shape deforms thousands of interior or surface vertices with a smooth, low-dimensional edit.

The coordinate family determines behavior. Mean-value and harmonic coordinates emphasize smooth interpolation; Green coordinates also account for cage-face normals and can better reproduce affine and detail-preserving deformation. A poor cage can still fold, invert, or create unintuitive global influence.

equations.label: Generalized barycentric reconstruction
equations.expression: x = Σ_j φ_j(x) c_j,   Σ_j φ_j(x)=1
terms: Rest-space weights φ_j reconstruct a point from cage controls c_j; animated controls produce x′.

sections.heading: Rig-based animation: hierarchy, skinning, IK, and retargeting
paragraphs: A rig separates control from deformation. A joint hierarchy evaluates local transforms into global bone transforms; skin weights map those transforms to the mesh; FK, IK, constraints, and controls let animators pose the hierarchy; retargeting maps motion between different skeleton proportions.

Automatic rigging predicts or fits a skeleton, while automatic skinning assigns influences. They are related but different optimization problems. The supplied term GX is preserved below, but it is not a standardized rigging acronym in the cited specifications or papers; a project must define it explicitly before it can be implemented.

equations.label: Linear blend skinning
equations.expression: x′ᵢ = Σ_j wᵢj (G_j B_j⁻¹) xᵢ,   Σ_j wᵢj=1
terms: G_j is the current global joint transform and B_j the bind transform.

equations.label: Jacobian IK update
terms: J⁺ is a pseudoinverse or damped least-squares inverse.

sections.heading: Skin deformation: correctives, helper bones, and muscle
paragraphs: Skin deformation begins where basic skinning fails. Helper bones distribute twist or preserve a silhouette; pose-space correctives add sculpted offsets at difficult joint configurations; muscle and flesh systems model bulging, sliding, volume, and secondary motion beneath the skin.

These layers should be ordered deliberately: skeleton motion provides the pose, muscles or volumetric tissue generate structure, helper transforms and correctives repair art-directed regions, and the final skin surface is evaluated for collision and rendering.

sections.heading: Hair simulation: rods, guides, and collisions
paragraphs: A hair strand is a slender elastic rod with stretch, bend, twist, damping, gravity, wind, and contact. Simulating every visible fiber is expensive, so production grooms animate sparse guide hairs and reconstruct follower motion while guarding against interpolation that cuts through the head or other strands.

Discrete elastic rods and Cosserat rods express orientation and curvature along the strand. Real-time methods simplify the model, solve constraints in parallel, or use neural surrogates, but collision and friction remain the difference between a convincing groom and a cloud of independent lines.

equations.expression: E = ½∫(k_s ε² + k_b|κ-κ₀|² + k_t(τ-τ₀)²) ds
terms: The terms penalize stretch ε, curvature κ, and twist τ.

sections.heading: Face animation: semantic controls and blend shapes
paragraphs: Face animation needs both fine geometry and interpretable controls. Blend shapes add weighted vertex deltas, joints handle jaw and eye motion, and FACS action units describe visible muscle actions independently of a particular character mesh.

Performance capture estimates these controls from video; audio-driven systems predict timing from speech; retargeting maps them to a new face. Correctives remain important because independently authored blend shapes are not linearly independent and combinations can collapse lips, cheeks, or eyelids.

sections.heading: Animation transformations: from keys to character motion
paragraphs: Animation transformations describe how values change through time and hierarchy. Translation, rotation, and scale form local TRS transforms; parent composition produces global motion; keyframes and splines define curves; blending combines clips; root motion and motion warping connect authored displacement to gameplay targets.

Rotation needs special treatment. Euler angles are readable but order-dependent and can gimbal lock; quaternions avoid that singular representation and support shortest-path spherical interpolation. Motion matching and generative motion choose or synthesize poses, but the selected pose still enters this deterministic transform pipeline.

equations.label: TRS composition
equations.expression: M_local = T(t) R(q) S(s),   M_global = M_parent M_local
terms: The engine's vector convention determines multiplication order, but it must be consistent.

equations.label: Quaternion SLERP
terms: cosΩ=q₀·q₁ after choosing the shortest quaternion sign.

aiResearch.summary: MotionCraft generates controllable character motion, MoMADiff focuses on multi-object interaction, and policy-space diffusion produces physics-based control policies. These models change how motion is proposed; transforms, interpolation, and blending still determine runtime execution.

closing: Vertex and cage systems control shape directly; rigs factor motion through a hierarchy and weights; correctives, muscle, hair, and facial systems restore the deformation that simple transforms cannot express; the runtime transform stack turns every authored or generated result into continuous motion. AI now automates capture, rigging, skinning, retargeting, and synthesis, but editable representations and deterministic evaluation remain the bridge from a research result to a production character.
